---
title: "GARCH Volatility Modelling: Extending the AAPL Forecasting Analysis"
format: html
---
## Introduction

In Project 1 I compared AR, MA and ARIMA models for AAPL daily prices and log returns. The models with the lowest AICc in both cases were the simplest ones, ARIMA(0,0,0) for the returns and ARIMA(0,1,0) for the price. The residual diagnostics of the returns model showed a problem. The Ljung-Box test on its residuals rejected white noise at the 5% level, but the same test on the squared residuals gave a far stronger result, statistic 74.81, p = 5.2e-12. This means the size of the errors was still correlated over time, so that large errors tended to be followed by large errors and small errors by small errors. An ARIMA model describes where a series is going next and assumes the spread around that forecast is the same in every period (course notes, Section 7.3.3), so it cannot represent this pattern.


ARCH and GARCH models were developed for this situation. They add a second equation that lets the conditional variance change over time, depending on recent squared errors and on the previous variance (Engle, 1982; Bollerslev, 1986, as presented in Sections 7.5 and 7.6 of the course notes). This project applies a GARCH(1,1) model to the same AAPL returns and asks two questions.

1. Does the GARCH model remove the volatility clustering that the ARIMA model left in the residuals?
2. Does it give better prediction intervals for out-of-sample returns, at horizons of 1, 5 and 20 trading days?


The second question concerns the intervals and not the point forecasts. Both the ARIMA and the GARCH model use a constant mean, so their point forecasts are both close to zero and small compared with the spread of the returns. The course notes make the same point about variance models in general, that what changes is the uncertainty attached to the forecast and not the forecast itself (Section 7.3.3). An ARIMA interval has the same width every day, whereas a GARCH interval should be wider after volatile days and narrower after calm days. A 95% interval should contain the actual return about 95% of the time, and I test whether this holds for each model, and for calm and volatile periods separately.


The data are the same as in Project 1: AAPL daily closing prices from [data source] between January 2017 and December 2019. The first 66% of the observations (to 21 December 2018) form the training set and the remaining observations (24 December 2018 onwards, about one year) form the test set. Keeping the same split as Project 1 allows the two projects to be compared directly, and it keeps the test set untouched until the models have been chosen.


The analysis follows the modelling workflow in Sulaiman Salau's ARCH and GARCH guide (Section 9) and Chapter 7 of the course notes: define the series, explore it, specify the mean, obtain the innovations, check for ARCH effects, specify the variance, estimate, diagnose, compare the models, and forecast and report. The mean equation is checked again under joint estimation with the variance equation. The notes warn that fitting the mean first and the variance to its residuals afterwards gives wrong standard errors (Section 7.10), and the mean chosen in Project 1 was selected under a constant-variance likelihood. The sections below follow the same order as the workflow.




## Define the Series
```{r setup}
set.seed(2026)
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(rugarch)
library(FinTS)
library(here)
library(ggplot2)

TICKER <- "AAPL"    
Start_date <- as.Date("2017-01-01")
End_date <- as.Date("2019-12-31")
train_frac <- 0.66

raw <- read_csv(
  here::here("data", "sp500_stocks.csv"),
  col_types = cols(date = col_date(format = "%Y-%m-%d"), symbol = col_character())
)

stock_window <- raw %>%
  filter(symbol == TICKER, date >= Start_date, date <= End_date) %>%
  arrange(date) %>%
  mutate(trading_day = row_number(),
         log_close = log(close),
         log_return = log_close - lag(log_close))


n_total <- nrow(stock_window)
n_train <- floor(n_total * train_frac)

train <- stock_window[1:n_train, ]
test <- stock_window[(n_train + 1):n_total, ]

returns_vec <- train$log_return[!is.na(train$log_return)]


```


The series modelled in this project is the daily log return of AAPL. Sulaiman Salau's guide lists defining the series as the first step of the workflow and asks for the sampling interval to be stated (Section 9), so I set out both here. The observations are daily closing prices on trading days between 3 January 2017 and 31 December 2019, 754 in total. There are no rows for weekends or public holidays, so consecutive observations are one trading day apart, and a return on a Monday covers the weekend. As in Project 1, I index the data by trading day and not by calendar date for this reason.

The variance equation describes the innovations around a conditional mean and not the level of a series, and the course notes list fitting a GARCH model to prices as a common mistake (Section 7.13). The training prices are also non-stationary, as Project 1 showed, ADF p = 0.96, KPSS p < 0.01, so I work with returns. The log return on day t is

r_t = log(P_t) - log(P_{t-1}),


where P_t is the closing price. This is the same return series as in Project 1. For small moves the log return is close to the simple percentage return (course notes, Section 7.3.1; Salau's guide, Section 2). Taking the first difference of the log price loses the first observation, so the 497 training prices give 496 training returns.


The data is split by time and not at random, so that the test set contains only days after every day used for fitting. The same split is used as in Project 1.

| Set | Trading days | First day | Last day |
|---|---|---|---|
| Training | 497 (496 returns) | 3 January 2017 | 21 December 2018 |
| Test | 257 | 24 December 2018 | 31 December 2019 |


Everything up to and including model selection uses only the training set. The test set is used at the end, to compare the one-day, five-day and 20-day forecast intervals of the two models. At a horizon of h days the target is the one-day return h trading days after the forecast origin, not the total return over those h days. The first test return is measured from the last training price, which is the return actually earned on the first test day. In the test period both models are refitted at each origin on all the returns up to that day, so no forecast uses data from after its origin.


The window is the same as in Project 1. It also suits this project, because the training returns include a long calm period through 2017 and the largest swings in the training set during the sell-off at the end of 2018, which is the kind of change in volatility that a variance model is meant to describe.


## Explore (Recap)

The full exploratory analysis of these returns is in Project 1, so this section only repeats the parts that the rest of this project relies on. These are the volatility clustering in the returns, the heavy tails, and the dependence in the size of the returns. Everything in this section uses the 496 training returns only.

```{r explore-recap}
plot(returns_vec, type = "l", col = "darkred",
     main = paste(TICKER, "- Training Set Log Returns"),
     xlab = "Trading Day", ylab = "Log Return")
abline(h = 0, lty = 2, col = "grey40")

```

The plot shows the 496 training returns against trading day, where day 250 is roughly the end of 2017. The returns move around zero with no trend, but the size of the swings is not constant. Most of 2017 is calm, apart from one large return of 0.059 near day 20. The swings get larger in early 2018, between around days 270 and 340, and again from about day 430, which is the last three months of the training set while the price was falling. The largest negative return, -0.069, is in this last stretch. Large returns come in groups and so do small ones, which is the volatility clustering listed with the stylised facts of financial returns (course notes, Section 7.3.2, Table 27; Salau's guide, Section 3).

```{r explore-summary}
m <- mean(returns_vec)
s <- sd(returns_vec)
data.frame(mean = m, sd = s,
           skewness = mean((returns_vec - m)^3) / s^3,
           kurtosis = mean((returns_vec - m)^4) / s^4)
```

The printed summary statistics are for the 496 training returns. The mean is 0.00059, about 0.06% a day, which is small compared with the standard deviation of 0.0147. A normal distribution has a kurtosis of 3, so a kurtosis of 5.92 means extreme returns happen more often than a normal distribution allows. These are the heavy tails listed with the stylised facts (course notes, Section 7.3.2, Table 27; Salau's guide, Section 3), and they are the reason I use a Student-t distribution for the innovations later in the project (course notes, Section 7.8). The skewness of -0.29 is mild, so the lower tail is only slightly longer than the upper tail.

```{r explore acf}
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
acf(returns_vec, lag.max = 20, main = "ACF of returns")
acf(returns_vec^2, lag.max = 20, main = "ACF of squared returns")
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

ci <- 1.96 / sqrt(length(returns_vec))
which(abs(acf(returns_vec^2, lag.max = 20, plot = FALSE)$acf[-1]) > ci)
```

The left plot shows the ACF of the returns. Most bars are inside the bounds of ±0.088, and the only ones outside are small bars at lags 7, 8, 10 and 17, the same lags as in Project 1. There is little linear dependence in the returns themselves. The ACF of the squared returns on the right is different. The printed check shows that 11 of the 20 lags are above the bound. Nine of them are in the first twelve lags, 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 8, 9, 11 and 12, and the other two are lags 17 and 20. About one bar in 20 would be outside the bounds by chance (course notes, Section 6.4), so eleven is far more than chance would give. The largest is at lag 6, at about 0.24. The bars do not decay smoothly, but every one of them is positive, so the dependence in the size of the returns lasts for many lags. This is the pattern in the stylised facts, where a series can be almost uncorrelated and still be predictable in its size (course notes, Section 7.3.2; Salau's guide, Section 3). It is the reason for fitting a model for the variance, and I test it formally in Check for ARCH Effects.


Project 1 also tested the training returns for stationarity. The ADF test rejected a unit root, p < 0.01, and the KPSS test rejected stationarity at the 5% level but not at the 1% level, p = 0.03. I put the KPSS result down to the changing variance seen above and not to a change in the mean, so the returns are treated as stationary in the mean and are not differenced again. The form of the mean equation is chosen in the next section.

## Specify the Mean
```{r joint mean comparison}
mean_orders <- list("(0,0)" = c(0,0),
                    "(1,0)" = c(1,0),
                    "(0,1)" = c(0,1),
                    "(1,1)" = c(1,1))

joint_results <- data.frame()

for (nm in names(mean_orders)){
    spec <- ugarchspec(
        variance.model = list(model = "sGARCH", garchOrder = c(1,1)), mean.model = list(armaOrder = mean_orders[[nm]], include.mean = TRUE), distribution.model = "std"
        )
    
    fit <- tryCatch(ugarchfit(spec = spec, data = returns_vec, solver = "hybrid"), error = function(e) NULL)
    if (is.null(fit)) next
  ic <- infocriteria(fit)
  joint_results <- rbind(joint_results, data.frame(
    MeanOrder = nm, AIC = ic["Akaike",], BIC = ic["Bayes",]
  ))


}

print(joint_results)

```


The mean equation in Project 1 was chosen with a likelihood that assumed the variance is constant. Now that the model has a variance equation, that choice should be checked again under the joint likelihood of both equations. The course notes warn that fitting the mean first and a GARCH model to its residuals afterwards gives reasonable coefficients but wrong standard errors (Section 7.10), and that the conditional mean should be right first, even if that means a constant (Section 7.13).

I fitted the same four mean specifications as in Project 1, an ARMA order of (0,0), (1,0), (0,1) and (1,1), each together with a GARCH(1,1) variance equation and Student-t innovations. Each model was estimated by maximum likelihood with ugarchfit(), so the mean and variance parameters were estimated at the same time, and the models were compared with AIC and BIC. The variance specification was the same in all four fits, so the only thing that changes between them is the mean equation.

The information criteria reported by rugarch are divided by the number of observations, which is why they are around -5.9 and not in the thousands. Lower values are better, and only the ordering and the differences matter. The constant-only mean (0,0) has the lowest AIC and the lowest BIC, and both criteria get worse as AR or MA terms are added. Multiplying the differences by the 496 observations puts them back on the usual scale: adding one AR or one MA term raises the AIC by about 1.8. An extra parameter costs 2 in the AIC penalty, so the extra term improved the log-likelihood by only about 0.1, which is almost nothing. The BIC penalises extra parameters more heavily and the gap is larger, about 6 for one extra term.

This agrees with Project 1, where the constant-only model was also selected under the constant-variance likelihood, and with the ACF of the returns in Explore, which showed no structure at the first few lags. For this series, adding the variance equation did not change the choice of mean. This fits the notes, which treat the conditional mean and the conditional variance as separate models of separate things (Section 7.14). The mean equation used in the rest of this project is therefore a constant.


## Obtain Innovations

```{r obtain innovations}
fit <- arima(returns_vec, order = c(0,0,0))
innovations <- residuals(fit)

cat("Mean estimate:", coef(fit), "\n")
cat("Number of innovations:", length(innovations), "\n")
```


The tests for ARCH effects are applied to the innovations of the mean model, because it is the variance of the innovations and not the variance of the raw series that is in question (course notes, Section 7.4). To get them I fitted the mean equation on its own, a constant-only model with no variance equation, using arima() with order (0,0,0). The innovations are the differences between each daily return and the fitted mean.

I fitted the mean on its own, with no variance equation, because the question at this step is whether a model that assumes a constant variance leaves structure in the size of its errors. This follows step 4 of Salau's workflow, which fits the mean model and examines its residuals before any variance model is specified (Section 9). Whether a variance equation removes that structure is a different question, and it is answered with the standardised residuals of the GARCH fits in Diagnose.

The fitted mean is 0.000588 per day, which is the sample mean of the training returns and matches the value in the summary statistics in Explore and in Project 1. The model gives 496 innovations, one for each training return. The innovations have a mean of zero by construction, and each one measures how far that day's return was from the average return. They are the input to the tests for ARCH effects in the next section.


## Check for ARCH Effects

```{r arch effects test}
arch_results <- ArchTest(innovations, lags = 12)
print(arch_results)

lb_squared <- Box.test(innovations^2, lag = 10, type = "Ljung-Box")
print(lb_squared)
```

Before fitting a GARCH model I check that one is needed, otherwise a variance equation would just be adding parameters to fit noise (course notes, Section 7.4). I ran two tests on the innovations from the previous step, Engle's ARCH LM test and the Ljung-Box test applied to the squared innovations. Both ask whether the size of past shocks helps predict the size of future ones. The Ljung-Box test on the squared residuals was already used in Project 1, while the ARCH LM test is new in this project.

Engle's test regresses the squared innovations on their own lags and compares n times the R-squared of that regression with a chi-squared distribution (course notes, Section 7.4). I used 12 lags, as in the example code in Salau's guide (Section 12). This gives chi-squared = 52.291, df = 12, p = 5.505e-07. The Ljung-Box test on the squared innovations at lag 10 gives X-squared = 74.81, df = 10, p = 5.2e-12. This is the same result as in Project 1's Diagnose section, since it tests the same thing, the squared residuals of a constant-mean model fitted to these training returns.

Both tests reject the null hypothesis of no ARCH effects, with p-values far below 0.01. This confirms formally what the returns plot and the ACF of the squared returns in Explore showed, that the variance of the innovations is not constant. A model that only specifies the mean therefore leaves structure in the variance behind. The tests do not say which variance model to fit (course notes, Section 7.4; Salau's guide, Section 10), so in the next section I compare an ARCH(1) and a GARCH(1,1) model.


## Specify the Variance

```{r specify variance}
arch1 <- ugarchspec(
    variance.model = list(model = "sGARCH", garchOrder = c(1,0)),
    mean.model = list(armaOrder = c(0,0), include.mean = T), 
    distribution.model = "std"
    )

garch11 <- ugarchspec(
    variance.model = list(model = "sGARCH", garchOrder = c(1,1)),
    mean.model = list(armaOrder = c(0,0), include.mean = T), 
    distribution.model = "std"
    )

fit_arch1 <- ugarchfit(spec = arch1, data = returns_vec, solver = "hybrid")
fit_garch11 <- ugarchfit(spec = garch11, data = returns_vec, solver = "hybrid")

show(fit_arch1)
show(fit_garch11)
```


## Estimate

I fitted two variance specifications on top of the constant mean. ARCH(1) is the simplest model that can represent volatility clustering, and GARCH(1,1) is the model the course notes recommend fitting first (Section 7.6). Comparing ARCH and GARCH models is step 6 of Salau's workflow (Section 9). Both models were specified with ugarchspec() and estimated by maximum likelihood with ugarchfit() on the 496 training returns, with Student-t innovations because of the heavy tails seen in Explore.

All parameters in both models are significant at the 5% level using the robust standard errors, which are the ones the course notes say to read (Section 7.8). The largest robust p-value is 0.032, for omega in GARCH(1,1). In ARCH(1), alpha1 = 0.60 is the weight on yesterday's squared shock, so one large return raises the next day's variance sharply. With no beta term, though, the model only remembers one day back (course notes, Section 7.5.3). In GARCH(1,1), alpha1 falls to 0.21 and beta1 = 0.78 carries the effect of a shock forward from day to day, so volatility reacts less sharply but fades slowly. Their sum, the persistence, is 0.9865, which I come back to in Forecast and Report. The Student-t degrees of freedom (shape) are 2.84 for ARCH(1) and 3.33 for GARCH(1,1), below the range of four to eight that the notes give as common for daily equity returns (Section 7.8), so the tails of these returns are heavy even for daily stock data.

GARCH(1,1) has the higher log-likelihood, 1458.03 against 1444.06, and the lower AIC, -5.859 against -5.807, and BIC, -5.817 against -5.773, so it is preferred on both criteria. Multiplied by the 496 observations, the AIC gap is about 26 and the BIC gap about 22. The one extra parameter, beta1, raised the log-likelihood by about 14, far more than the penalty for adding it. Salau's guide warns against choosing a model on information criteria alone (Section 13), so I check next whether the better fit also gives better-behaved residuals.


## Diagnose

Each fitted model was checked using its standardised residuals, the raw residuals divided by the model's own conditional standard deviation for that day. These are what the model claims are independent and identically distributed, so they are the residuals to test (course notes, Section 7.9). If the variance equation has captured the volatility clustering, the standardised residuals should show no leftover autocorrelation, in either their raw or squared form. The tests below are the weighted Ljung-Box and ARCH LM tests that rugarch prints with each fit.

Neither model shows autocorrelation in the standardised residuals up to lag 5, the longest lag rugarch reports for this test, ARCH(1) p = 0.58, GARCH(1,1) p = 0.48. These tests do not reach the small bars at lags 7, 8, 10 and 17 in the ACF of the returns, so they say nothing about those. The squared-residual and ARCH LM tests separate the two models. ARCH(1) passes the Ljung-Box test on its squared residuals but fails the ARCH LM test at lag 6, p = 0.019, so some volatility clustering is still left after fitting it, which the course notes read as ARCH effects that remain unmodelled (Section 7.9). GARCH(1,1) passes every squared-residual and ARCH LM test reported, up to lag 9, p = 0.94. GARCH(1,1) is therefore the model carried forward for the rest of this project.

The adjusted Pearson goodness-of-fit test compares the standardised residuals with the fitted Student-t distribution. For GARCH(1,1) its p-values are between 0.47 and 0.94 across the four groupings, so there is no evidence against the Student-t choice.

Two more diagnostics apply to both models. The Nyblom test rejects the null hypothesis that the parameters are constant for both ARCH(1), joint statistic 3.31 against a 5% critical value of 1.24, and GARCH(1,1), 5.85 against 1.47, and both are also above the 1% critical value. For GARCH(1,1) the individual statistics point to alpha1, beta1 and the shape parameter, while omega and mu are below their critical values. The training period ends with the sell-off in the last three months of 2018, which could be a change in the level of volatility partway through the sample. The course notes warn that a break of this kind pushes the estimated persistence towards one (Section 7.12), which matters for the persistence of 0.9865 found above. I did not refit the model on parts of the training set to test this, so I come back to it as a limitation in the Discussion.

The Sign Bias test is not significant for either model, joint effect p = 0.67 for ARCH(1) and 0.82 for GARCH(1,1), so there is no evidence that negative shocks raise volatility more than positive shocks of the same size. The notes suggest fitting the symmetric model first and only moving to an asymmetric one if the asymmetry is significant (Section 7.11), so I keep the symmetric GARCH(1,1).

## Compare Models (Part A: Residual Problem / Part B: Interval Calibration)

```{r compare models}
garch11_residuals <- residuals(fit_garch11, standardize = TRUE)

lb_before <- Box.test(innovations^2, lag = 10, type = "Ljung-Box")
lb_after <- Box.test(garch11_residuals^2, lag = 10, type = "Ljung-Box")

comparison <- data.frame(
    Model = c("ARIMA(0,0,0) only (Project 1)", "GARCH(1,1) standardized residuals"),
    X_squared = c(lb_before$statistic, lb_after$statistic),
    p_value = c(lb_before$p.value, lb_after$p.value)
)

print(comparison)
```

Part A answers the first question, whether GARCH(1,1) removes the problem left by the ARIMA model. In Project 1 the residuals of the ARIMA(0,0,0) model failed the Ljung-Box test once squared, showing that the size of the errors was still correlated over time, and this was confirmed again in Check for ARCH Effects. I apply the same test at the same lag (10) to two sets of residuals, the squared innovations of the mean-only model and the squared standardised residuals of GARCH(1,1).

The statistic falls from 74.81 to 3.29 and the p-value rises from 5.2e-12 to 0.97, so there is no evidence of autocorrelation left in the squared residuals up to lag 10 once they are standardised. The GARCH variance equation accounts for the volatility clustering that the ARIMA model could not represent. This is an in-sample result. The model was fitted to these same data, so it shows the model does what it is designed to do, but not that it forecasts better. That is tested out of sample in Part B.


### Part B

```{r coverage-test}
returns_full <- stock_window$log_return[-1]
n_train <- length(returns_vec)
n_total <- length(returns_full)

origins <- seq(n_train, n_total - 1, by = 1)

results_coverage <- data.frame()

for (i in origins) {
    data_sub <- returns_full[1:i]
    actual <- returns_full[i + 1]

    fit_a <- tryCatch(arima(data_sub, order = c(0,0,0)), error = function(e) NULL)
    if (!is.null(fit_a)) {
        fc_a <- predict(fit_a, n.ahead = 1)
        arima_lower <- fc_a$pred[1] - 1.96 * fc_a$se[1]
        arima_upper <- fc_a$pred[1] + 1.96 * fc_a$se[1]
        arima_covered <- actual >= arima_lower & actual <= arima_upper
        arima_width <- arima_upper - arima_lower
    } else {
        arima_covered <- NA
        arima_width <- NA
        arima_lower <- NA
        arima_upper <- NA
    }

    spec_i <- ugarchspec(
        variance.model = list(model = "sGARCH", garchOrder = c(1,1)),
        mean.model = list(armaOrder = c(0,0), include.mean = TRUE),
        distribution.model = "std"
    )
    fit_g <- tryCatch(ugarchfit(spec = spec_i, data = data_sub, solver = "hybrid"), error = function(e) NULL)

    if (!is.null(fit_g)) {
        fc_g <- ugarchforecast(fit_g, n.ahead = 1)
        g_mean <- as.numeric(fitted(fc_g))
        g_sigma <- as.numeric(sigma(fc_g))
        df_t <- coef(fit_g)["shape"]
        tq <- qdist("std", p = 0.975, shape = df_t)
        garch_lower <- g_mean - tq * g_sigma
        garch_upper <- g_mean + tq * g_sigma
        garch_covered <- actual >= garch_lower & actual <= garch_upper
        garch_width <- garch_upper - garch_lower
    } else {
        garch_covered <- NA
        garch_width <- NA
        garch_lower <- NA
        garch_upper <- NA
        g_sigma <- NA
        df_t <- NA
    }

    results_coverage <- rbind(results_coverage, data.frame(
        origin = i, actual, arima_lower, arima_upper, arima_covered, arima_width, garch_lower, garch_upper, garch_covered, garch_width, garch_sigma = g_sigma, garch_df = df_t
    ))
}

coverage_summary <- data.frame(
    Model = c("ARIMA(0,0,0)", "GARCH(1,1)"),
    Coverage = c(mean(results_coverage$arima_covered, na.rm = TRUE),
                 mean(results_coverage$garch_covered, na.rm = TRUE)),
    Avg_Width = c(mean(results_coverage$arima_width, na.rm = TRUE),
                  mean(results_coverage$garch_width, na.rm = TRUE)),
    n_origins = c(sum(!is.na(results_coverage$arima_covered)),
                  sum(!is.na(results_coverage$garch_covered)))
)
print(coverage_summary)
```

Part B answers the second question, whether GARCH(1,1) gives better prediction intervals out of sample, which Salau's guide gives as the preferred way to compare volatility models (Section 9, step 9). I built one-day-ahead 95% prediction intervals for every day in the test period. At each origin both models were refitted on all the returns up to that day, the interval for the next day was computed, and the actual return was checked against it. This gives 257 origins. The ARIMA interval is the forecast mean plus or minus 1.96 times the fitted constant standard deviation. The GARCH interval uses that day's forecast standard deviation and the 97.5% quantile of the standardised Student-t distribution with the fitted shape, which is the interval the course notes give for a model with a GARCH variance (Section 7.7.4).

Both models are close to the 95% target. ARIMA covers 94.16% of the test returns and GARCH 94.94%, which is 242 and 244 of the 257 days, so the difference is two days. With 257 origins the standard error of a coverage estimate near 95% is about 1.4 percentage points, so a gap of 0.8 points is well within sampling noise, and on overall coverage neither model is better. The GARCH intervals are also about 10% wider on average, 0.068 against 0.062, so GARCH does not reach the same coverage with narrower intervals.

```{r conditional coverage}

med_sigma <- median(results_coverage$garch_sigma, na.rm = TRUE)
high <- results_coverage$garch_sigma > med_sigma

cond_coverage <- data.frame(
    regime = c("Low predicted volatility", "High predicted volatility"),
    ARIMA = c(mean(results_coverage$arima_covered[!high]), mean(results_coverage$arima_covered[high])),
    GARCH = c(mean(results_coverage$garch_covered[!high]), mean(results_coverage$garch_covered[high])), 
    n = c(sum(!high), sum(high))
)

print(cond_coverage)

```

Overall coverage can hide a difference between calm and volatile days. The course notes point out that one fixed interval width is too wide in calm periods and too narrow in volatile ones (Section 7.3.3). To check this I split the 257 origins into two halves by GARCH's own forecast standard deviation for the next day, which is known before the return is observed, and computed the coverage of both models in each half.

In the calm half ARIMA covers 97.67% of the returns, more than it should, and in the volatile half only 90.63%, which is the pattern Section 7.3.3 describes for a fixed width. GARCH covers 96.12% and 93.75%, closer to 95% in both halves. In counts, GARCH misses four fewer days than ARIMA in the volatile half (8 against 12 of 128) and two more in the calm half (5 against 3 of 129). Each half has about 128 days, so the standard error of each coverage figure is about 2 percentage points, and the gaps between the models are of a similar size to that. The volatile days also come in runs, because volatility clusters, so they are not independent, and there is only one test year. The result fits GARCH's intervals adapting to changing volatility at the one-day horizon, but it is not strong enough on its own to show this.


```{r interval plot}
plot_df <- results_coverage
plot_df$date <- stock_window$date[-1][plot_df$origin +1]

ggplot(plot_df, aes(x = date)) +
    geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = garch_lower, ymax = garch_upper), fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.3) + 
    geom_line(aes(y = arima_lower), colour = "darkred", linetype = "dashed") +
    geom_line(aes(y = arima_upper), colour = "darkred", linetype = "dashed") +
    geom_point(aes(y = actual), size = 0.7) +
    labs(title = "AAPL 1-day-ahead 95% prediction intervals (test period)",
         subtitle = "Blue band: GARCH(1,1)-t. Dashed red: ARIMA(0,0,0)",
         x = "Date", y = "Log return")


```

The plot shows the one-day-ahead 95% intervals over the test period, GARCH(1,1) as the blue band and ARIMA(0,0,0) as the dashed red lines. The ARIMA lines stay almost flat at about ±0.03, because each refit gives nearly the same constant standard deviation. The GARCH band is widest in the first weeks of the test period, reaching about ±0.10 in early January 2019. It then narrows through February and March and for much of the year is close to, and at times narrower than, the ARIMA lines, before widening again after large returns in May and in August. Some returns fall outside both intervals, most clearly the return of about -0.10 in early January 2019. GARCH misses 13 of the 257 days and ARIMA 15, against about 13 expected for a 95% interval, so a few misses are what these intervals allow for. The GARCH band widens after a large return has happened, not before it. The one-day forecast variance is built from the latest squared shock, which is already known at the origin (course notes, Section 7.7.1), so the model reacts to a shock and does not anticipate one.


```{r horizon-coverage}
#| cache: true
horizons <- c(1, 5, 20)
max_h <- max(horizons)

n_r_train <- length(returns_vec)
n_r_total <- length(returns_full)
origins <- seq(n_r_train, n_r_total - 1, by = 1)

res_list <- list()

for (i in origins) {
    data_sub <- returns_full[1:i]

    fit_a <- tryCatch(arima(data_sub, order = c(0,0,0)), error = function(e) NULL)
    if (!is.null(fit_a)) fc_a <- predict(fit_a, n.ahead = max_h)

    spec_i <- ugarchspec(
        variance.model = list(model = "sGARCH", garchOrder = c(1,1)),
        mean.model = list(armaOrder = c(0,0), include.mean = TRUE),
        distribution.model = "std"
    )
    fit_g <- tryCatch(ugarchfit(spec = spec_i, data = data_sub, solver = "hybrid"),
                      error = function(e) NULL)
    if (!is.null(fit_g)) {
        fc_g <- ugarchforecast(fit_g, n.ahead = max_h)
        g_mean <- as.numeric(fitted(fc_g))
        g_sigma <- as.numeric(sigma(fc_g))
        tq <- qdist("std", p = 0.975, shape = coef(fit_g)["shape"])
    }

    for (h in horizons) {
        if (i + h > n_r_total) next
        actual <- returns_full[i + h]
        one_row <- data.frame(origin = i, h = h, actual = actual,
                              arima_covered = NA, arima_width = NA,
                              garch_covered = NA, garch_width = NA,
                              garch_sigma = NA)
        if (!is.null(fit_a)) {
            lo <- fc_a$pred[h] - 1.96 * fc_a$se[h]
            hi <- fc_a$pred[h] + 1.96 * fc_a$se[h]
            one_row$arima_covered <- actual >= lo & actual <= hi
            one_row$arima_width <- hi - lo
        }
        if (!is.null(fit_g)) {
            lo <- g_mean[h] - tq * g_sigma[h]
            hi <- g_mean[h] + tq * g_sigma[h]
            one_row$garch_covered <- actual >= lo & actual <= hi
            one_row$garch_width <- hi - lo
            one_row$garch_sigma <- g_sigma[h]
        }
        res_list[[length(res_list) + 1]] <- one_row
    }
}
results_h <- do.call(rbind, res_list)

horizon_summary <- do.call(rbind, lapply(horizons, function(h) {
    d <- results_h[results_h$h == h, ]
    data.frame(Horizon = h,
               ARIMA_coverage = mean(d$arima_covered, na.rm = TRUE),
               GARCH_coverage = mean(d$garch_covered, na.rm = TRUE),
               ARIMA_width = mean(d$arima_width, na.rm = TRUE),
               GARCH_width = mean(d$garch_width, na.rm = TRUE),
               n_origins = sum(!is.na(d$garch_covered)))
}))
print(horizon_summary)
```

I repeated the exercise for 5-day-ahead and 20-day-ahead intervals, to check whether the pattern at one day carries over to longer horizons. As set out in Define the Series, the target at horizon h is the one-day return h trading days after the origin. For ARIMA(0,0,0) the forecast standard deviation is the same at every horizon, while GARCH uses its forecast standard deviation for day h, which moves towards the model's long-run level as h grows (course notes, Section 7.7.2).

ARIMA's coverage and width hardly change with the horizon, 94.16%, 94.47% and 94.96%, with a width of 0.062 throughout, because its interval uses the same standard deviation however far ahead it forecasts. GARCH's average width grows from 0.068 at one day to 0.075 at five days and 0.093 at twenty days, and its coverage rises from 94.94% to 96.84% and then 97.48%. At the longer horizons the GARCH intervals contain more returns than a 95% interval should, so they are wider than they need to be.


```{r horizon-conditional}
cond_h <- do.call(rbind, lapply(horizons, function(h) {
    d <- results_h[results_h$h == h & !is.na(results_h$garch_sigma), ]
    high <- d$garch_sigma > median(d$garch_sigma)
    data.frame(Horizon = h,
               Regime = c("Low predicted volatility", "High predicted volatility"),
               ARIMA = c(mean(d$arima_covered[!high]), mean(d$arima_covered[high])),
               GARCH = c(mean(d$garch_covered[!high]), mean(d$garch_covered[high])),
               n = c(sum(!high), sum(high)))
}))
print(cond_h)

tapply(results_h$garch_sigma, results_h$h, mean)
sd(returns_full[-(1:length(returns_vec))])

```

Splitting the origins by GARCH's forecast standard deviation for day h shows where the extra width goes. At five days GARCH covers 96.03% of the volatile half against 91.27% for ARIMA, and both models cover 97.64% of the calm half. At twenty days the pattern changes. GARCH covers 99.16% of the volatile half, well above 95%, and 95.80% of the calm half. ARIMA now covers close to 95% in both halves (94.12% and 95.80%). ARIMA's interval has the same width every day, so its coverage in each half shows how large the actual returns in that half were. At one day the volatile half had clearly more large returns than the calm half, but at twenty days it did not, so GARCH's twenty-day forecast no longer picks out the days on which large returns happened.

The reason is the GARCH forecast path. The mean GARCH forecast standard deviation rises with the horizon, from 0.0182 at one day to 0.0200 at five days and 0.0249 at twenty days, while the standard deviation of the test returns is 0.0170. GARCH forecasts revert towards the long-run level implied by the fitted parameters, from below when volatility is lower than that level (course notes, Section 7.7.2). For the training fit that level is 0.0352 (Forecast and Report, Part A), more than twice the standard deviation of the training returns. The long-run variance is omega divided by one minus the persistence (Salau's guide, Section 7). With a persistence of 0.9865 that denominator is only 0.0135, so a small change in alpha1 or beta1 moves the long-run level a lot. Estimate showed this high persistence, and Diagnose found that the parameters were not stable across the training window, so the long-run level that the twenty-day forecasts move towards is the least reliable part of the model. The short-horizon results should therefore not be carried over to long-horizon volatility forecasts without more checking.

## Forecast and Report

### Part A

```{r garch parameters}

cf <- coef(fit_garch11)
omega <- as.numeric(cf["omega"])
alpha1 <- as.numeric(cf["alpha1"])
beta1 <- as.numeric(cf["beta1"])

persistence <- alpha1 + beta1
half_life <- log(0.5) / log(persistence)
long_run_var <- omega / (1 - persistence)

print(c(persistence = persistence, half_life_days = half_life, long_run_sd = sqrt(long_run_var), sample_sd = sd(returns_vec)))


```

As shown in Estimate, the GARCH(1,1) model has alpha1 = 0.207 and beta1 = 0.780, so the persistence is alpha1 + beta1 = 0.9865. Persistence this close to 1 means a volatility shock fades slowly. The half-life, log(0.5)/log(0.9865), is about 51 trading days, or roughly ten weeks (Salau's guide, Section 7). The long-run daily standard deviation implied by the parameters, sqrt(omega / (1 - persistence)), is 0.0352, more than twice the standard deviation of the training returns, 0.0147. I do not read 0.0352 as a realistic long-run volatility for AAPL. Salau's guide warns that persistence close to one describes the fitted model and sample and does not establish permanent volatility (Section 13), and Diagnose found that the parameters were not stable over the training window. The long-run level still matters, though, because GARCH forecasts move towards it as the horizon grows, which is why the twenty-day intervals in Compare Models were too wide.

### Part B

```{r garch forecast path}

fc_path <- ugarchforecast(fit_garch11, n.ahead = 20)
sigma_path <- as.numeric(sigma(fc_path))
arima_sd <- sqrt(fit$sigma2)

plot(1:20, sigma_path, type = "b", pch = 16,
     ylim = range(c(sigma_path, arima_sd, sqrt(long_run_var))),
     xlab = "Horizon (trading days)", ylab = "Forecast conditional sd",
     main = "GARCH(1,1) volatility forecast from end of training")
abline(h = arima_sd, lty = 2, col = "darkred")
abline(h = sqrt(long_run_var), lty = 3, col = "grey40")

```

The plot shows the GARCH(1,1) forecast of the daily standard deviation of the log return, made at the end of the training set for 1 to 20 trading days ahead. The forecast starts at about 0.029 and rises slowly to about 0.031 by day 20. The dashed red line is the constant standard deviation of the ARIMA(0,0,0) model, 0.0147, and the dotted grey line is the long-run level, 0.0352. The forecast starts well above the ARIMA line because volatility was high at the end of the training set, after the sell-off. It rises rather than falls because that level is still below the long-run level, and GARCH forecasts move towards the long-run level from wherever volatility is at the origin (course notes, Section 7.7.2). So straight after the sell-off the model forecasts volatility to go up further, which comes from the high long-run level. From this origin the rise is small, because 20 days is well under the half-life of about 51 days. From calmer origins later in the test period, where volatility was far below 0.0352, the rise over 20 days is larger, which is why the mean twenty-day forecast in Compare Models was 0.0249 against 0.0182 at one day.


```{r vol forecast vs actual}
vol_df <- results_coverage
vol_df$date <- stock_window$date[-1][vol_df$origin + 1]
vol_df$arima_sd <- (vol_df$arima_upper - vol_df$arima_lower) / (2 * 1.96)

ggplot(vol_df, aes(x = date)) +
    geom_point(aes(y = abs(actual)), size = 0.8, colour = "grey30") +
    geom_line(aes(y = garch_sigma), colour = "steelblue", linewidth = 0.9) +
    geom_line(aes(y = arima_sd), colour = "darkred", linetype = "dashed") +
    labs(title = "AAPL test period: realised |return| vs forecast volatility",
         subtitle = "Blue: GARCH(1,1)-t one-day-ahead sigma. Dashed red: ARIMA(0,0,0) constant sd",
         x = "Date", y = "|Log return| / forecast sd")
```

This plot compares the one-day-ahead forecasts with what happened in the test period. The blue line is the GARCH one-day-ahead forecast standard deviation, the dots are the absolute values of the returns on each day, and the dashed red line is the ARIMA standard deviation. The GARCH line jumps to about 0.054 in early January 2019, after the large returns at the start of the test period, and then falls back over the following weeks. Smaller rises follow later large returns, most clearly in May and in August. In calmer stretches, such as March to April and October to December, the GARCH line is below the ARIMA line, so its intervals on those days are narrower. As in the interval plot, each rise comes after a large return and not before it.


```{r vol fitted in sample}
in_df <- data.frame(date = train$date[-1],
                    abs_return = abs(returns_vec),
                    garch_sigma = as.numeric(sigma(fit_garch11)))

ggplot(in_df, aes(x = date)) +
    geom_point(aes(y = abs_return), size = 0.8, colour = "grey30") +
    geom_line(aes(y = garch_sigma), colour = "steelblue", linewidth = 0.9) +
    labs(title = "AAPL training period: realised |return| vs fitted GARCH volatility",
         x = "Date", y = "|Log return| / fitted sd")
```

The same comparison over the training period shows the fitted volatility, so here the model has already seen the data. The fitted line follows the clusters of large returns, including the rise during the sell-off in the last months of 2018, where it reaches about 0.037. For most of the training period it is between about 0.01 and 0.025. The long-run level of 0.0352 is above the fitted volatility on almost every training day, so it is not a level the series spent much time at, which supports not reading it as AAPL's long-run volatility.


```{r price and vol}
dates_ret <- stock_window$date[-1]
n_tr <- length(returns_vec)

price_df <- data.frame(date = stock_window$date,
                       value = stock_window$close,
                       panel = "AAPL close price ($)")

vol_train <- data.frame(date = dates_ret[1:n_tr],
                        value = as.numeric(sigma(fit_garch11)),
                        panel = "GARCH volatility (sd)")

vol_test <- data.frame(date = dates_ret[results_coverage$origin + 1],
                       value = results_coverage$garch_sigma,
                       panel = "GARCH volatility (sd)")

combined <- rbind(price_df, vol_train, vol_test)
combined$period <- ifelse(combined$date <= max(train$date),
                          "Training (in-sample fit)",
                          "Test (one-day-ahead forecast)")

ggplot(combined, aes(x = date, y = value, colour = period)) +
    geom_line() +
    geom_vline(xintercept = as.numeric(max(train$date)), linetype = "dashed") +
    facet_grid(panel ~ ., scales = "free_y") +
    labs(title = "AAPL price and GARCH(1,1) conditional volatility",
         x = "Date", y = NULL, colour = NULL)

c(train_mean = mean(returns_vec),
    test_mean = mean(returns_full[-(1:length(returns_vec))]))
```

The last figure puts the closing price and the GARCH volatility on the same time axis. The price rises from about $27 at the start of training to a peak near $55 around October 2018, falls to about $36 by the end of training, and then rises through the test period to about $70 by the end of 2019. The volatility rises in the last months of 2018 as the price falls, reaches about 0.054 at the start of the test period, higher than anything in training, and then falls back to between about 0.012 and 0.015 for most of 2019, with smaller rises in May and August. The training part of the volatility line (teal) is the in-sample fit, while the test part (coral) is the one-day-ahead forecast made with only the data up to the day before. Volatility went up while the price fell in late 2018 and came down as the price recovered in 2019, but I do not read this as a leverage effect, because the Sign Bias test in Diagnose found no significant difference between the response to negative and positive shocks.

## Discussion

This project asked two questions about the AAPL returns. The first was whether a GARCH(1,1) model removes the volatility clustering that the ARIMA(0,0,0) model in Project 1 left in its residuals. The ARCH LM test and the Ljung-Box test on the squared innovations both confirmed the clustering was there, p = 5.5e-07 and p = 5.2e-12. After fitting GARCH(1,1), the Ljung-Box statistic on the squared standardised residuals fell from 74.81 to 3.29, p = 0.97, and the model passed every squared-residual and ARCH LM test that rugarch reports, up to lag 9. ARCH(1) did not, failing the ARCH LM test at lag 6, which fits the notes' point that one day of memory is the central weakness of ARCH(1) (Section 7.5.3). So for the training data the answer is yes. This is an in-sample result, since the model was checked on the data it was fitted to, so it shows the variance equation does what it is designed to do but says nothing yet about forecasting. Taken together with Project 1, where AR and MA terms did not improve on a constant mean, the structure left in AAPL's daily returns over this window was mainly in the size of the returns and not in their direction.

The second question was whether GARCH(1,1) gives better prediction intervals out of sample at 1, 5 and 20 trading days. At one day the two models had almost the same overall coverage, 94.94% for GARCH against 94.16% for ARIMA, a difference of two days out of 257. Split by GARCH's forecast volatility, ARIMA covered too many returns on calm days, 97.67%, and too few on volatile days, 90.63%, as the course notes expect for a fixed interval width (Section 7.3.3), while GARCH stayed closer to 95% in both halves, 96.12% and 93.75%. At five days the gap in the volatile half was larger, 96.03% against 91.27%, although GARCH covered the calm half no better than ARIMA, 97.64% each. These gaps are of a similar size to their standard errors and come from one test year, so they are consistent with GARCH adapting its intervals to recent volatility but do not prove it. At twenty days the GARCH intervals were too wide, covering 97.48% of returns overall and 99.16% of the volatile half. Their mean forecast standard deviation was 0.0249, against 0.0170 for the test returns, because the forecasts move towards a long-run level of 0.0352, more than twice the training standard deviation. So the answer to the second question is a qualified one. At short horizons GARCH gives intervals that respond to recent volatility, without a clear gain in overall coverage, and at twenty days its intervals depend on a long-run level that I do not trust.

These results have several limits. First, the training window ends with the sell-off at the end of 2018, and the Nyblom test found that the parameters of both models were not stable across it. The course notes warn that a break in the level of volatility pushes the estimated persistence towards one (Section 7.12), and a higher persistence gives a higher long-run level, so a break could be part of why the long-run level came out at 0.0352. I did not refit the model on parts of the training set to check this. Second, everything comes from one stock and one test year, and the volatile days in that year come in runs, so the coverage results by regime rest on a small number of days that are not independent. Third, the test period had a much higher average return than the training period, 0.0027 a day against 0.0006. Both models use a mean estimated on the training data, so neither anticipates this. The effect on interval coverage is small, because a difference of about 0.002 is small next to a daily standard deviation of 0.015 to 0.017. It matters more for forecasts of the price, and it is why the positive mean in the returns branch helped it beat the price branch in Project 1. Finally, I only compared ARCH(1) and a symmetric GARCH(1,1), both with Student-t innovations. The Sign Bias test gave no reason to fit an asymmetric model, but I did not fit one to check. The first thing I would add is a refit of the model on the calm and volatile parts of the training set, to see whether the persistence and the long-run level drop once the sell-off is separated out.
